It also corrected an overclaim in the LLM-AGY-001 rationale: the cited AgentRuntime.kt comment locates a gate-handling mechanism, it does not establish the required absence-of-gate element. The governing evidence boundary, tightened in round 2 and held since, is: each row's affirmative_architecture_split may cite only (a) content of the row's own evidence_scope anchor file (including its comments and docstrings), and (b) that same file's own direct local imports (module-level or function-scoped import statements written in the anchor file itself). A file discovered by finding who calls the anchor file (a reverse caller), by a repository-wide search/find for a plausibly-related file, or by opening a package-internal file that is not itself the direct target of an import statement (e.g. a schema file inside an npm-imported package whose import surface only exposes a client object) is NOT admissible as affirmative cross-module proof, even if it is real, relevant, and was in fact opened during investigation.

For each row, the applicable rule's required-evidence checklist (docs/packs/free-llm-v1-rule-contract.md) is applied to what is admissible per the boundary above: does the anchor file itself (its own content, or a file it directly imports) contain every element the checklist requires (file_local), does it concretely and admissibly establish that ALL required elements are resolvable well enough to conclude the checklist is definitely not satisfiable within the anchor file alone (cross_module, non-ambiguous -- full-chain treatment, adopted in round 3), or does neither hold within the admissible boundary (ambiguous)? Round 3 clarified that partial resolution -- e.g. proving only one of a multi-element rule's required elements is external -- is NOT sufficient for a confident classification. Round 4 clarified a further, previously inconsistently-applied corollary: a required element is not 'resolved' merely because a second file is named via a genuine import statement and its name or surrounding context plausibly suggests it carries that element -- the citation must be backed by content this document actually read and quoted establishing the element, not by inference from the imported module's name (e.g. 'claim_extractor' sounding claim-extraction-related, or 'ModelProber' sounding like it invokes a model). Round 4 also treats a second-component citation whose own recorded rationale explicitly admits uncertainty (e.g. 'must be inspected to confirm') as, by that admission, an unresolved element, not a confident one.

A row is recorded file_local only when every required element is textually present or locally defined in the anchor file itself. A row is recorded cross_module, non-ambiguous, only when the full required-evidence chain for the applicable rule is admissibly resolvable from the anchor file's own content and/or its own direct imports -- a concrete second file named via an admissible path, substantively relevant to the required element(s) it is cited for (an import present in the file but used only for something unrelated to the rule's checklist -- e.g. an unrelated output-directory constant -- does not count), backed by content actually read (not merely an import statement plus a plausible module name), and sufficient to resolve every required element of the applicable rule's checklist, not merely one or some of them. A row is recorded ambiguous, with classification held at the conservative cross-module fallback and ambiguous=true, whenever the only available evidence is a reverse caller, a same-package/same-directory sibling with no import statement connecting the two, a repository-wide search discovery, a package-internal file not itself the import target, an admissible citation resolving only part of a multi-element required-evidence chain, or a citation resting on an imported module's name/context rather than its actually-read content -- even when that partial evidence is real and was actually inspected.
